query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibits 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but inadequate oxygen resistance prevents most practical high-temperature applications. Earlier oxidation-protection research prevented pesting in a related, non-equiatomic Hf–Nb–Ta–Ti–Zr alloy during a 5 h exposure to air at 800 °C, but that result does not establish protection for equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr; related studies on other refractory alloys likewise did not evaluate this composition. With preservation of useful room- and high-temperature mechanical performance as a design constraint, what single intervention could improve the oxygen resistance of equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr? Formulate one hypothesis identifying the intervention and mechanism, predicting the outcome relative to untreated material, defining the applicable temperature, atmosphere, exposure-time, and loading boundaries, citing supporting evidence from the prior studies, and specifying a controlled experiment and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A minor addition of aluminum (around 2 atomic percent) to the cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy will form a continuous, adherent alumina (Al2O3) scale during high‐temperature exposure in air, significantly improving its oxygen resistance while preserving its room- and elevated-temperature mechanical performance.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr alloy with documented 8–16% room-temperature ductility and yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C.
generation.intervention: Modify the alloy composition by adding approximately 2 at% aluminum during casting.
generation.conditions: Exposure to air at 800 °C for 5 hours (conditions similar to earlier oxidation-protection studies on related alloys), with mechanical performance remaining comparable to untreated material under room and high-temperature regimes.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a thin, continuous, and adherent alumina (Al2O3) scale on the alloy surface.
generation.mechanism: Aluminum has a high affinity for oxygen, and its presence in the alloy promotes the in situ formation of a protective Al2O3 layer during high-temperature oxidation. This barrier significantly reduces oxygen ingress (and thus oxidation) while the low concentration minimizes impacts on the alloy’s bulk mechanical properties.
generation.predicted_outcome: The aluminum-doped alloy will show a markedly reduced oxidation rate and less structural degradation (pesting) at 800 °C over 5 hours compared to the untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr, with minimal changes in its tensile ductility and high-temperature yield strength.
generation.baseline: Untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy, which exhibits inadequate oxygen resistance under the same conditions (exhibiting rapid oxidation and pesting).
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is applicable for high-temperature (around 800 °C) air exposure over a few hours (e.g. 5 h), and under testing conditions that do not impose mechanical loads beyond those used in standard tensile tests for these materials.
generation.uncertainty: The precise aluminum concentration required to form an optimal protective alumina scale without affecting phase stability, microstructure, or mechanical performance is uncertain, and potential interactions with existing elements need to be carefully monitored.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of cast alloy samples: one set of equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr with a 2 at% Al addition and one set of the untreated baseline alloy. Process both identically. Subject samples to air exposure at 800 °C for 5 hours. Then, compare the degree of oxidation (via mass gain measurements and oxide scale thickness evaluated using SEM/EDS) and assess mechanical properties via room- and high-temperature tensile tests.
measurements: Mass gain per unit area (as an index of oxidation rate)
Oxide scale thickness and continuity (by SEM/EDS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the aluminum-doped samples do not show a statistically significant reduction in oxidation (lower mass gain and thinner or more adherent oxide scale) compared to the baseline, or if the mechanical performance (ductility and yield strength) is significantly degraded relative to the untreated alloy under the defined conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloy was chosen to analyze the effect of each constituent elemental by the subtraction method and, thus, HfMoNbTaTiZr, HfNbTaTiZr, HfMoTaTiZr, HfMoNbTiZr, HfMoNbTaZr, and HfMoNbTaTi were studied. Among these alloys, HfMoNbTaTi has the best mechanical performance, that is, 27% compressive strain at room temperature and yield strength 367 MPa at 1400 °C. HfMoNbTaTi has great potential for elevated-temperature applications. As the alloy system does not contain very expensive elements such as Re and Ru, it is cost competitive for high-temperature applications like Nb-Hf-Ti alloys in space vehicles. Further modification of composition and/or anti-oxidation coatings are still required for high-temperature applications in the air. According to the experiment results, the effects of Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr on mechanical properties of equiatomic Hf-Mo-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr alloys were described. For higher room-temperature strength, one should add an element which interacts frequently with the alloy, such as Mo.
